source: Curated student game fragment: missed mate on the back rank
student_message: I played 1.g3 to make luft. Why was that not best?
engine_refutation: 1.g3 lets Black answer ...g6, giving the king luft and removing the immediate back-rank mate. White missed 1.Re8#.
reference_explanation: The student solved a slow safety problem while a forcing checkmate was available. The coach should explain that checks come before quiet improvements: Black's king is trapped by its own f-, g- and h-pawns, so 1.Re8# ends the game immediately. The habit correction is to scan all checks and mate threats before making a useful-looking move.
key_ideas: look at checks before quiet moves
do not improve when mate is available

source: Curated student game fragment: missed checking fork
student_message: I pushed 1.b4 to gain space and keep the knight protected. What did I miss?
engine_refutation: After 1.b4 Black can simply take or move away from the fork motif, while 1.Nc7+ wins the queen by force.
reference_explanation: The key feature is that the knight has a checking fork. 1.Nc7+ attacks the king and queen at the same time, so Black must answer the check and cannot save the queen. The student's pawn move is too slow because it ignores a forcing tactic that wins decisive material immediately.

source: Curated student game fragment: developing while mate is available
student_message: I played 1.Nc3 because development matters. Was that too routine?
engine_refutation: 1.Nc3 misses the immediate 1.Qxf7#. After the routine move, Black can defend f7 and the forced mate is gone.
reference_explanation: Development is normally good, but concrete tactics override principles. The queen can take f7 with mate because the bishop on c4 protects the queen and the king has no escape. The coach should teach the student to ask whether there is an immediate checkmate before playing a normal developing move.
key_ideas: Qxf7 is defended by the bishop

source: Curated student game fragment: automatic queen promotion
student_message: I promoted to a queen automatically. Why is 1.c8=Q wrong here?
engine_refutation: 1.c8=Q does not win the queen on e7. 1.c8=N+ is the engine move because the new knight checks the king and forks the queen.
reference_explanation: The mistake is assuming every promotion should be a queen. Here the knight promotion is stronger because it comes with check and attacks the queen on e7. The coach should train the habit of comparing all promotion pieces when a knight promotion can give check or fork.

source: Curated student game fragment: queen mate technique
student_message: I kept checking with the queen. I tried 1.Qe3. What is the problem with that plan?
engine_refutation: 1.Qe3+ keeps checking but does not improve the mating net. The engine's 1.Kf3 brings the king closer, which is the clean winning technique.
reference_explanation: In queen versus king, random queen checks are less important than building a box and bringing the king up. The student's queen move keeps playing with one piece. The coach should explain that the winning habit is to coordinate king and queen while avoiding stalemate.

source: Curated student game fragment: king-and-pawn opposition
student_message: I played 1.Kd5 because I wanted to escort the pawn. Why does that throw away the win?
engine_refutation: 1.Kd5 lets the defender contest the key squares. The winning method is 1.Kd6 or 1.Kf6, keeping the king on the sixth rank in front of the pawn.
reference_explanation: The student moved the king away from the winning key-square zone. In king and pawn endings, the stronger king must occupy the sixth-rank key squares in front of the pawn. The coach should diagnose the misconception that simply staying near the pawn is enough.

source: Curated student game fragment: square of the pawn
student_message: I played 1.Kg7 first to bring my king closer. Why should I push the pawn instead?
engine_refutation: 1.Kg7 wastes a tempo. The engine move 1.a6 uses the fact that the black king is outside the pawn's square and cannot catch it.
reference_explanation: The student failed to count the square of the pawn. The black king is too far away, so the passed pawn promotes by force if White starts running immediately. The coach should teach the square rule as a fast objective check before moving the king.

source: Curated student game fragment: Philidor defense mistake
student_message: As Black I checked from behind with 1...Rh1. Why is that premature?
engine_refutation: 1...Rh1 abandons the third-rank defense too early and lets White's king advance. 1...Rh6 keeps the Philidor draw.
reference_explanation: In the Philidor position the defender should first keep the rook on the third rank to stop the attacking king from reaching the sixth. The student's checking move starts the checking phase before the pawn has advanced, giving up the drawing setup. The coach should name the defensive rule: third rank first, rear checks only later.

source: Curated student game fragment: Lucena bridge mistake
student_message: I played 1.Re1 to get ready to block checks. What did I miss in the Lucena?
engine_refutation: 1.Re1 does not drive the black king away. The engine move 1.Rf2+ first gains the checking tempo needed to build the bridge.
reference_explanation: The student knows the bridge idea but skipped the forcing first step. In Lucena, the stronger side must first check the defending king away, then bring the rook to the fourth rank to block checks. The coach should separate the plan into its ordered technique: check first, bridge second.

source: Curated student game fragment: smothered mate move order
student_message: I jumped in with 1.Nf7+. Why does the queen sacrifice have to come first?
engine_refutation: After 1.Nf7+ Black can answer 1...Rxf7, removing the knight. The engine move 1.Qg8+ forces ...Rxg8, blocking the escape square before Nf7#.
reference_explanation: The student saw the mating pattern but used the wrong move order. The queen sacrifice on g8 forces the rook to occupy g8, trapping the king completely; only then does Nf7 mate. The coach should praise the pattern recognition while correcting the forcing sequence.
